articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Question: Where the Tourist Tax Actually Goes
articles.dek: Bed tax revenues hit record highs last fiscal year. A Flightline review of spending records shows most of it never touches the beach.
brief: Escambia County collected $47.2 million in tourist development tax revenue in fiscal year 2025, a 12% increase over the previous year
Only 23% of expenditures went to Pensacola Beach infrastructure and maintenance, while downtown Pensacola projects received 34%
State law requires tourist tax funds promote tourism, but allows broad interpretation of what qualifies
articles.body:
The numbers live in a spreadsheet buried three clicks deep on the Escambia County website. No press release announced them. No commissioner held a news conference.

But the figures tell a story worth $47.2 million.

That's how much Escambia County collected in tourist development tax revenue last fiscal year—money generated when visitors pay an extra 5% on hotel rooms, vacation rentals and campground stays. The haul marked a 12% jump from fiscal year 2024 and set a new record for the county.

Where that money went is another matter.

A Flightline review of county expenditure reports, budget documents and Tourist Development Council meeting minutes reveals a spending pattern that sends most bed tax dollars away from the beaches that generate them. Of the $41.3 million the county spent from the tourist development fund in fiscal year 2025, just $9.5 million—23%—went to Pensacola Beach infrastructure, maintenance and improvements.

Downtown Pensacola received $14.1 million. That's 34% of total expenditures.

Following the Money

The tourist development tax exists under Florida Statute 125.0104, which allows counties to levy the charge for purposes that promote tourism. The law is deliberately broad. It permits spending on convention centers, sports facilities, beach maintenance and "tourism promotion."

Escambia County interprets that mandate generously.

The largest single expenditure last year was $8.2 million for debt service on the Pensacola Bay Center. The arena, located downtown on East Gregory Street, hosts concerts, trade shows and Pensacola Ice Flyers hockey games. County records classify this as tourism infrastructure.

Visit Pensacola, the county's destination marketing organization, received $6.8 million for advertising, staff salaries and operations. The organization's headquarters sit on West Garden Street, 12 miles from Pensacola Beach.

Another $4.7 million went to the Pensacola Sports Association for event recruitment and facility grants. That money helped bring amateur softball tournaments to Vickrey Resource Park and soccer events to Ashton Brosnaham Park—both located in the county's interior, miles from any shoreline.

Beach Money, Beach Problems

Pensacola Beach operates under a peculiar arrangement. The Santa Rosa Island Authority, a state-created entity, manages the beach but relies heavily on county tourist tax allocations for capital projects.

SRIA Executive Director Paolo Ghio declined a recorded interview but confirmed by email that the authority requested $14.2 million from the county for fiscal year 2025. It received $9.5 million.

"We work with what we're allocated," Ghio wrote.

That allocation covered lifeguard operations, beach maintenance equipment and a portion of the ongoing Casino Beach restroom renovation. It did not fully fund the authority's request for additional parking infrastructure on Via de Luna or repairs to the Quietwater Beach boardwalk.

Both projects remain on a waiting list.

Meanwhile, beach visitors continue generating the bulk of tourist tax revenue. Visit Pensacola's own research, presented at a February TDC meeting, showed that 71% of overnight visitors to Escambia County cite beaches as their primary reason for coming. The same presentation noted that average daily spending among beach visitors exceeds that of downtown visitors by $47 per person.

The Legal Question

Whether this spending pattern violates state law depends on how you read the statute.

"The law says you can spend on things that promote tourism," said David Flagg, a Tallahassee-based attorney who has litigated tourist tax disputes in other Florida counties. "It doesn't say you have to spend it where the tourists actually go."

Flagg, who reviewed the Escambia expenditure breakdown at The Flightline's request, said the county's spending appears legally defensible if not necessarily logical.

"You could argue the Bay Center brings people to town who then go to the beach," he said. "You could argue marketing campaigns benefit everyone. Whether that's the best use of the money is a policy question, not a legal one."

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose District 1 includes Pensacola Beach, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Neither did County Administrator Wes Moreno.

Commissioner Lumon May, who represents a district that includes downtown Pensacola, offered a brief statement through a spokesperson: "The Tourist Development Council makes recommendations. The commission weighs many factors in final allocations."

Who Decides

The Tourist Development Council is a nine-member advisory board that recommends how bed tax money should be spent. State law requires its membership include hotel operators, vacation rental managers and tourism industry representatives.

Six of the current nine members have business interests in downtown Pensacola or the county's interior. Three represent beach-area businesses.

TDC Chair Marcus Webb owns a boutique hotel on Palafox Street. Vice Chair Dana Reeves operates an event venue in the Warehouse District. Member appointments are made by county commissioners.

Webb did not return a phone call seeking comment.

The council meets monthly in a conference room at the Visit Pensacola offices. Meetings are public but not televised. Minutes are posted online, typically three to four weeks after each session.

At the May 2026 meeting, the most recent for which minutes are available, the council voted 7-2 to recommend maintaining current allocation percentages for fiscal year 2027. The two dissenting votes came from beach-area representatives.

What the Numbers Say

Escambia County's tourist tax spending looks different from its neighbors.

In Okaloosa County, which includes Destin and Fort Walton Beach, 52% of tourist development tax expenditures in fiscal year 2025 went directly to beach nourishment, maintenance and infrastructure. Another 18% funded the county's destination marketing organization. The county collected $38.7 million in bed tax revenue.

In Bay County, home to Panama City Beach, the split was 61% beach-related, 22% marketing. Revenue totaled $29.4 million.

Escambia's 23% beach allocation ranks lowest among major tourism-dependent counties in Northwest Florida.

County budget documents offer no explanation for the disparity. The tourist development tax section of the fiscal year 2025 budget runs four pages and contains no narrative discussion of allocation philosophy or priorities.

Looking Ahead

The county commission will vote on fiscal year 2027 tourist development tax allocations at its September budget hearings. The TDC's recommendation maintains the status quo: roughly one-quarter to beach interests, one-third to downtown projects, the remainder split among marketing, sports and debt service.

SRIA's Ghio said the authority plans to request $16.1 million—a 70% increase over current allocations. The request includes $4.2 million for parking improvements and $2.8 million for Quietwater Beach infrastructure.

Whether commissioners will deviate from the TDC recommendation is unclear. In the past five years, the full commission has modified TDC spending recommendations exactly once, in 2023, when it shifted $300,000 from marketing to beach lifeguard operations after a drowning death received extensive media coverage.

The public comment period for the fiscal year 2027 budget opens August 15. The county has scheduled two hearings: September 8 and September 22, both at 5:30 p.m. in the Ernie Lee Magaha Government Building.

The spreadsheet will be updated sometime after that.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: The Warehouse District's Quiet Transformation
articles.dek: Between the railroad tracks and Main Street, a dozen buildings have changed hands in 18 months. The buyers aren't local.
brief: At least 12 properties in Pensacola's Warehouse District have sold since January 2025, with most buyers registered to LLCs in Miami, Atlanta, and Nashville
Combined sale prices exceed $14 million, nearly triple the assessed values of the properties
Long-term tenants including three artist studios and a specialty food distributor have received lease non-renewals
articles.body:
The loading dock at 415 West Intendencia Street still smells like roasted coffee. For eleven years, Gulf Coast Coffee Collective operated here, buying green beans from small farms and selling to restaurants from Mobile to Panama City. The roasters are gone now. So are the burlap sacks stacked against the brick walls, the sample jars lined up on wooden shelves, the hand-painted sign that read "Pensacola's Bean" in faded yellow letters.

What remains is a 6,400-square-foot shell with original heart pine floors, 16-foot ceilings, and new owners based in Coral Gables.

"They gave us ninety days," said Marcus Trent, who co-founded the roasting operation in 2015. "Said they had other plans for the space. Wouldn't say what."

The coffee collective's departure in April was one of at least eight commercial tenant exits from the Warehouse District since fall 2025. Property records obtained by The Flightline show a pattern: buildings purchased by out-of-state limited liability companies, followed within months by lease non-renewals for existing tenants.

Following the Paper Trail

The Warehouse District occupies roughly twelve square blocks between West Main Street and the CSX railroad tracks, bounded by Alcaniz Street to the east and DeVilliers Street to the west. Once home to cotton warehouses, fish processing plants, and marine supply operations, the area has housed a mix of light industrial businesses, artist studios, and small manufacturers for decades.

Escambia County property records show 14 commercial sales in this zone since January 2025. Twelve of those transactions involved buyers registered to addresses outside Florida.

The largest single purchase: a 22,000-square-foot former ice plant on West Zarragossa Street, sold in March 2025 for $2.8 million to Harbor Point Development LLC. The company's registered agent lists a Nashville address. The previous owner, a Pensacola family that had held the property since 1987, sold it for roughly four times its 2024 assessed value.

Harbor Point Development did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Other buyers include Meridian South Holdings, registered in Atlanta, which purchased three adjacent buildings on West Government Street totaling $3.1 million. A Miami-based entity called Coastal Legacy Partners acquired the former Gulf Coast Coffee building and two neighboring structures for a combined $2.4 million.

Coastal Legacy Partners' registered agent, attorney David Menendez, declined to discuss specific plans. "Our clients are evaluating options for the properties," he said by phone. "That's all I can say at this time."

The Tenants Left Behind

Rosa Delgado spent nine years building her ceramic studio at 308 West Intendencia. She taught classes three nights a week, fired commissioned pieces for restaurants and hotels, and stored her kilns in a back room that leaked when it rained.

In February, her landlord—a Pensacola dentist who had owned the building since 2003—sold to Meridian South Holdings. Six weeks later, Delgado received a certified letter informing her that her lease would not renew past July 31.

"I asked if I could stay month-to-month while I found a new place," Delgado said. "They said no. They said they needed the building vacant."

She has since relocated to a smaller space in Ferry Pass, sharing kiln access with another artist. Her Tuesday evening beginner classes, which once drew 15 students, now max out at six.

Similar stories emerged across the district. Coastal Provisions, a specialty food distributor supplying olive oils and imported cheeses to area restaurants, closed its Warehouse District location in May after 14 years. Owner Beth Carney said the new building owners declined to negotiate a new lease.

"They were perfectly polite about it," Carney said. "But they made clear they weren't interested in keeping a food warehouse. They kept saying 'highest and best use.' I heard that phrase probably five times."

Carney now operates from a climate-controlled storage unit near the airport, fulfilling orders at half her previous volume.

What Comes Next

No formal development applications have been filed with the City of Pensacola for any of the recently sold Warehouse District properties, according to city planning department records reviewed by The Flightline.

Pensacola's downtown development coordinator, James Whitfield, said his office has not been contacted by representatives of the new ownership groups.

"We'd welcome those conversations," Whitfield said. "The Warehouse District is part of our urban core, and we want to see it activated. But we can't require property owners to share their intentions with us."

City zoning maps show the area classified as "Commercial Intensive," which permits a range of uses from retail and restaurants to light manufacturing and residential lofts. Building height limits of 65 feet apply to most parcels.

Real estate analysts who spoke with The Flightline said the purchase prices and buyer profiles suggest repositioning for higher-value uses—likely some combination of residential, hospitality, or mixed-use development.

"You don't pay three to four times assessed value for a warehouse you plan to keep as a warehouse," said Catherine Odom, a commercial appraiser based in Mobile who tracks the Gulf Coast market. "These are speculative acquisitions. The buyers are betting on Pensacola's trajectory."

That trajectory has been steep. Downtown Pensacola's residential population roughly doubled between 2015 and 2024, according to Census Bureau estimates. Hotel occupancy rates have consistently exceeded 70 percent since 2022. The Pensacola Bay Center, located less than a mile from the Warehouse District, draws over 400,000 visitors annually.

A Familiar Pattern

Long-time downtown business owners see echoes of earlier transitions.

Martin Suarez has operated Suarez Metalworks on West Government Street since 1998, fabricating custom railings, gates, and architectural details. His building, a 4,200-square-foot brick structure his father purchased in 1982, has not sold. But three of his neighbors' buildings have.

"I remember when they said Palafox was going to change, back in the early 2000s," Suarez said, standing in his shop's open bay door on a recent afternoon. "They were right. Rents went up. The old businesses moved out or closed. Now it's all restaurants and boutiques."

He paused, watching a delivery truck navigate the narrow street. "I'm not saying that's bad. Palafox is nice now. But it's not the same place. And some of those people who built it up—they're not there anymore."

Suarez said he has received two unsolicited offers to purchase his building in the past year, both from out-of-state buyers. He declined both.

"I'm sixty-two," he said. "I figure I've got maybe eight more years of climbing ladders and swinging hammers. After that, who knows. But I'm not ready to hand it over yet."

Waiting for Answers

On a Thursday evening in late June, the 400 block of West Intendencia sat mostly dark. The former coffee collective's windows were papered over. Delgado's old studio had a commercial lockbox on the door. The only active business was a screen-printing shop at the end of the block, its fluorescent lights visible through a propped-open door.

Inside, owner Kevin Marsh was running a batch of t-shirts for a local brewery. He has operated from the same location for seven years. His lease runs through December 2027.

"I've got eighteen months of certainty," Marsh said over the hum of the press. "After that, I honestly don't know. Nobody's told me anything. Nobody's told anybody anything."

He pulled a fresh shirt from the press, checked the print, and set it aside.

"That's the thing that gets me," he said. "All this money moving around, all these buildings changing hands. And none of us who actually work here have any idea what's coming."

The Flightline will continue to monitor development applications and property transactions in the Warehouse District. Readers with information about planned projects can contact us at tips@theflightline.com.

articles.label: Local News
articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Week Brings 200,000 Visitors and a Strained Infrastructure
articles.dek: With the July show days away, Pensacola Beach braces for its biggest weekend of the year while road construction on Via de Luna remains unfinished.
brief: The Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show July 10-11 is expected to draw over 200,000 visitors to Pensacola Beach, marking the largest annual event in Escambia County.
Via de Luna Drive construction delays have left a 0.8-mile stretch between Avenida 10 and Avenida 18 reduced to one lane in each direction through the weekend.
Santa Rosa Island Authority officials are urging visitors to arrive before 7 a.m. or use the free shuttle system from the Pensacola Bay Center.
articles.body:
The orange barrels start at Avenida 10 and stretch east for nearly a mile. On a Tuesday afternoon, a single flagman waves traffic through the construction zone on Via de Luna Drive, the only road connecting Pensacola Beach to the rest of the world. In four days, this same stretch will carry tens of thousands of cars toward the Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show.

The timing is not ideal.

"We knew the risk," said Paolo Ghio, executive director of the Santa Rosa Island Authority, during a Monday briefing. "The contractor assured us they'd have both lanes open by July 8. That's not going to happen."

The road project—a $2.3 million drainage improvement and repaving effort awarded to Pensacola-based Gulf Coast Paving in February—was scheduled for completion by June 15. Supply chain delays for concrete pipe pushed the timeline back. Then came the rain. Escambia County recorded 14.2 inches in June, the wettest on record since 1997.

Now the authority faces a logistical puzzle: how to funnel an estimated 200,000 visitors onto a 40-foot-wide island over a road that's been cut in half.

The biggest weekend

The Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show remains the largest annual event in Northwest Florida. The Navy's flight demonstration squadron, based at Naval Air Station Pensacola since 1949, performs its only Gulf Coast show of the year over the beach each July.

Last year's event drew an estimated 185,000 spectators across two days, according to Visit Pensacola. Hotel occupancy in Escambia and Santa Rosa counties hit 94 percent. Short-term rental bookings on the beach itself reached full capacity three months in advance.

This year's crowd could be larger. The Blue Angels are flying a new demonstration routine for the first time since 2021, and the show falls on a Friday-Saturday instead of last year's Thursday-Friday schedule.

"We've already exceeded last year's booking pace by about 12 percent," said Darien Schaefer, president and CEO of Visit Pensacola. "The economic impact should be somewhere north of $25 million for the weekend."

That money comes with traffic.

One road in, one road out

Pensacola Beach sits on Santa Rosa Island, a barrier island accessible only by the Bob Sikes Bridge from Gulf Breeze. Via de Luna Drive runs the length of the developed portion of the island, serving as the main artery for residents, tourists, and emergency vehicles alike.

Under normal conditions, the road handles about 15,000 vehicles per day during summer weekends. On Blue Angels weekend, that number can triple.

The Santa Rosa Island Authority has managed show-day traffic for decades. The standard playbook includes extended bridge hours, temporary no-parking zones, and a free shuttle system from the Pensacola Bay Center downtown.

This year, the construction complicates everything.

Gulf Coast Paving will suspend work from Thursday evening through Sunday morning, according to Escambia County spokeswoman Laura Coale. Traffic cones and barrels will be moved to the shoulder. But the road surface between Avenida 10 and Avenida 18 remains unfinished—ground to bare asphalt in preparation for the final layer that won't be laid until mid-July.

"It's passable, but it's rough," Coale said. "We're asking people to slow down through that section."

The county has added temporary signage warning of the road conditions. The speed limit through the construction zone drops to 25 mph.

Shuttle or suffer

Island authority officials are pushing the shuttle system harder than in previous years. The free buses run from the Pensacola Bay Center parking garage starting at 8 a.m. both days, with service continuing until two hours after the show ends.

"If you're not staying on the beach, take the shuttle," Ghio said. "I cannot stress this enough. If you drive over after 9 a.m., you will sit in traffic for two hours minimum."

The authority has also expanded its partnership with Escambia County Area Transit. Additional buses will run the Route 62 line from downtown Pensacola to the beach, with service every 15 minutes during peak hours.

For those who insist on driving, Ghio offered blunt advice: arrive before 7 a.m. or watch from somewhere else.

"The casino beach parking lot will be full by 8," he said. "Portofino lot, same thing. After that, you're parking a mile east and walking."

The view from the sand

The show itself remains free. Spectators can watch from anywhere along the public beach. The flight demonstration typically runs from approximately 2 p.m. to 3 p.m. each day, with civilian aerobatic acts and military flyovers filling the earlier afternoon hours.

Practice sessions are scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday, offering a preview for those who want to avoid the weekend crowds. The team typically runs a full dress rehearsal Thursday afternoon that mirrors the Saturday performance.

Food and beverage vendors will line Casino Beach and Quietwater Boardwalk. Alcohol is permitted on the beach but glass containers are prohibited.

The National Weather Service forecast for Friday and Saturday shows partly cloudy skies with temperatures in the low 90s and afternoon heat indices approaching 105 degrees. Scattered thunderstorms—the usual summer pattern—could develop after 4 p.m. both days but are not expected to affect the demonstration times.

After the smoke clears

Gulf Coast Paving is scheduled to resume work on Via de Luna the Monday after the show. The current contract calls for final completion by July 31, though Coale acknowledged that timeline is now "aspirational."

The road project is one of several infrastructure improvements underway on the island. A separate $1.8 million water main replacement on Fort Pickens Road wrapped up in May. A third project—stormwater improvements near the Margaritaville hotel—is scheduled to begin in September.

For now, the focus is getting through the weekend.

"We do this every year," Ghio said. "The road situation isn't ideal, but we'll manage. We always do."

The Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show runs Friday, July 10 and Saturday, July 11. Gates at Casino Beach open at 8 a.m. The flight demonstration begins at approximately 2 p.m. both days. For shuttle information and parking updates, visit visitpensacolabeach.com.
